Chapter 5: Media, Representation, and the Power of Narrative
Picture this: you flip on the TV, scan through a newspaper, or scroll your social feed, and the stories you see? They’re almost always coming from just one perspective. The faces in charge, the voices you hear setting the agenda, the images shaping what we all think—most of them are white. And if you don’t see yourself reflected in those spaces, the message hits hard: your story just doesn’t seem to matter as much.
Imagine being a teenager, looking for someone to look up to, but barely seeing anyone who looks like you in the headlines or on screen. And when Black people do show up? It’s usually in stories about crime, poverty, or failure. That might sound subtle, but it’s incredibly powerful—it quietly shapes how people see themselves, and how others see them too.
The truth is, media has a huge influence on the way we all think about race. The stories we hear—and just as importantly, the ones we never hear—shape everything from the policies leaders make to the way we treat each other every day. When the only images of Black communities are negative, it becomes so much easier to justify unfair treatment, and a lot harder to picture something better.
Most folks don’t realize just how much control the media has over what’s seen as normal, desirable, or even possible. And because newsrooms and production teams so often lack diversity, some stories just never get told… or they get told in ways that only reinforce harmful stereotypes.
Think about a journalist who wants to cover a story about racism. They might feel pressure to chase the most sensational angle, rather than dig into the real issues. Editors worry about turning readers off, or about being accused of bias. So what happens? The coverage often ends up feeling shallow, a bit defensive, and it misses what truly matters.
For people who are misrepresented—or ignored altogether—the impact is real, and it’s painful. Challenging injustice gets so much harder when the public conversation is controlled by people who don’t understand, or maybe just don’t care, about the realities of racism. And that keeps the cycle of misunderstanding and denial spinning.
But here’s some hope: things are starting to shift. More and more people are speaking up, calling for better representation, and finding new ways to share their own stories. The real challenge now? It’s moving beyond token gestures, and building a media landscape where everyone’s experiences matter, and where the true complexity of British life is visible for all to see.
The power of narrative—of telling stories—is massive. When we change which stories get told, we change how people see themselves, and each other. It’s not a quick fix, but it’s absolutely essential if we want a society that’s fair, open, and equal.
